title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.

title: Live Herd Maps for Hiking Apps
one_liner: Collar-derived herd positions pushed to hiking and mountain-bike apps so hikers reroute around cattle, funded by the destination that profits from the landscape.
customer: Alpine and mountain destination bodies, municipalities and trail associations paying for a valley licence. Secondary buyers are livestock-liability insurers and the trail apps themselves as distribution partners.
problem: Cattle-hiker incidents have produced large liability judgments in the Alps (reported in Tyrol and elsewhere), pushing farmers to fence trails or abandon high pastures, which erodes the landscape tourists come for. Hiker density is rising with overtourism. The farmer knows where the cows are, and virtual-fencing and GPS collars already record it, but the hiker does not.
solution: Ingest positions from virtual-fencing and GPS collars and cheap satellite or LoRa tags, and publish geofenced herd zones at roughly 30-minute freshness through an open API to trail apps such as Outdooractive, Komoot, AllTrails and Gaia. Add trailhead QR and SMS warnings and detour suggestions. The incident log becomes the farmer's dated proof of warnings issued, which supports liability cover and premium credits. A US variant covers guardian-dog and cattle conflicts on western grazing allotments.
why_now: Virtual-fencing collars (Halter, Nofence) have scaled from pilots to fleets, and satellite IoT now covers valleys without cell service. International arrivals hit about 1.52B in 2025, and Spain, Italy and Japan are all trying to move visitors off crowded routes. Destinations have new levies and budgets to spend on dispersal.
revenue_model: EUR12K-EUR40K/yr per valley from destination bodies. A collar-vendor or farmer data fee of EUR3-EUR6 per collar per month. Insurer data licences and app API fees.
non_obvious_insight: The herd data is a by-product already collected for a different reason, and the liability problem is fundamentally an information problem. Selling to the destination rather than the farmer solves who pays, because the destination's product is the pastoral landscape.
first_30_days: Pick one valley (Tyrol, Graubunden or Colorado) with an existing collar deployment, and sign the destination body and farmers' cooperative to a summer-2027 pilot by March. Build a GPX geofence feed and get one trail app to test it as a data partner.

title: Mobile Cobot Safety Validation Lab
one_liner: A van-based lab that measures collision forces and signs off robot and cobot cells against the 2025 ISO 10218 revisions.
customer: Cobot distributors, integrators and 10-200 person manufacturers deploying cells. EHS managers and insurers are the second buyers.
problem: North American robot orders are broadening into semiconductors, pharma and food, and cobots are 15.4% of units. The 2025 revisions of ISO 10218-1 and -2 (which absorbed the collaborative guidance of ISO/TS 15066) require documented risk assessment and validation. Few engineers can do it, and force-measurement gear costs tens of thousands of dollars. Distributors skip validation and the liability lands on the shop and its insurer.
solution: A van with a calibrated force and pressure measurement device, safety-scanner zone tester and stop-time tester. Technicians validate on site (contact-force mapping by body region, speed and separation checks) and deliver a signed report. Software stores and versions results for audits. Annual revalidation is a subscription.
why_now: Revised standards are in force, robot demand is broadening to small shops and new sectors, and mobile manipulators are coming into plants.
revenue_model: $2.5-6k per cell validation. White-label contracts with distributors. About $1.2k a year for revalidation. Referral fees from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The limiting step for small-shop robots is fear of liability, not price. A third-party validation stamp is what insurers and owners want, and distributors have the incentive to sell but not the independence or equipment to certify.
first_30_days: Rent or buy a used force-measurement device. Sign three cobot distributors. Complete a machinery functional-safety credential. Validate the first five cells at a discount.

title: Buy the Orphaned License of Dead Models
one_liner: Acquire or secure exclusive commercial-licensing rights to hugely downloaded open models and tools whose company died, then sell clean, warranted commercial licenses plus a public orphan-license registry.
customer: Startups and mid-size companies shipping voice features (dubbing, audiobooks, IVR, game NPC voices, accessibility) on top of XTTS-class models, and the procurement or legal teams of their enterprise buyers who now ask for model-license provenance.
problem: Coqui XTTS-v2 is still pulled about 6.75M times a month under a non-commercial license (CPML), but Coqui shut down in Dec 2023. Commercial licensing was 'available upon inquiry' from a company that no longer exists, so builders either violate the license, ship legal risk to customers, or rip out the best multilingual voice-cloning model. GitHub threads asking about commercial use or the license after shutdown were closed 'wontfix'.
solution: Phase 1: trace the rights chain (Coqui Inc., founders, assignees, any bankruptcy or dissolution filings) and option an exclusive commercial-licensing agency deal or outright IP purchase, which should be cheap because the seller is a dead startup. Phase 2: sell per-product annual commercial licenses ($2k-$25k) with a written rights-chain warranty and an audit letter that customers can hand to enterprise procurement. Phase 3: publish an Orphan Model Registry (model, steward status, license, who can grant commercial rights) as a free lead-gen asset and a paid API for AI-governance tools. Fallback if the rights-holder refuses: sell a fixed-price license-risk audit and a swap-to-permissive-model migration (Apache/MIT TTS) with regression tests.
why_now: Enterprise AI-governance questionnaires in 2026 ask for model and data provenance. The $1.5B Anthropic authors settlement (2025) and the Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (HN front page 2026-09-27, 626 points) made license hygiene a board-level topic. Open voice tools are exploding: VoiceStudio hit 43.9k stars, +27k in one month, and its README warns each bundled model has its own license to review before commercial use.
revenue_model: Annual per-product licenses ($2k-$25k), enterprise-wide licenses, audit and migration fees ($3k-$8k fixed price), registry API subscription ($200-$1k a month).
non_obvious_insight: Demand is already proven and supply is literally zero: nobody can sell a commercial license because the seller is dead, so dead-startup IP is the scarcest cheap asset in open AI. Evidence: XTTS-v2 shows 6,752,613 downloads last month under CPML (https://huggingface.co/coqui/XTTS-v2). Coqui repo issues on commercial use, license after shutdown and 'Move to MIT' are closed wontfix (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues?q=commercial+license+is%3Aissue). Issue #4022, opened nearly a year after shutdown, says the community is confused about 'commercial use and fine-tuning' (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues/4022). HN, Nov 2023: XTTS stays non-commercial with commercial licensing 'upon inquiry'. VoiceStudio's AGPL repo warns model licenses vary (https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio).
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull Delaware and other corporate records for Coqui Inc., message the founders and former staff, and draft a one-page option agreement (small cash plus revenue share). Days 1-10: build the registry from 50 popular non-commercial or orphaned models on Hugging Face. Days 10-30: email companies that opened XTTS licensing issues and companies whose products visibly use XTTS (from public GitHub dependency graphs) with a $3k risk audit, and aim for 3-5 paid audits. If the rights option lands, convert those audits into licenses.

title: Flat-Fee Guarantee Against Runaway Agent Bills
one_liner: Pay a few percent on top of model spend and the guarantee absorbs any overnight blowout above a hard multiple of baseline, enforced by an inline kill switch.
customer: AI-native startups and agencies spending $5k-$200k per month on model and tool calls (seed to Series B), including dev shops deploying agents for clients.
problem: Retry loops turn $0.40 tasks into $40, and five-figure overnight bills are reported. Blended token prices fell about 67% in a year but agentic workflows burn 5-30x more tokens, and 73% of enterprises overran AI budgets. The market sells dashboards and caps. Nobody sells a promise, and founders and their investors want the tail risk gone.
solution: A drop-in proxy (change one base URL) that sees all model and tool traffic and learns a rolling baseline per agent and workflow. The guarantee covers spend above a set multiple of baseline in a rolling window (for example 4x over 6 hours), up to a cap, paid as cash or credits. The proxy enforces circuit breakers so maximum loss is bounded, which makes underwriting tractable. Coverage applies only where default breaker policies were accepted, which controls moral hazard.
why_now: TechCrunch was covering the scramble over runaway AI costs by June 2026. Gateways are being absorbed into security suites (Palo Alto bought Portkey), and dozens of cap-and-alert tools have commoditized enforcement without offering a guarantee.
revenue_model: 3-6% premium on metered spend plus a gateway subscription, with parametric or MGA reinsurance for large limits.
non_obvious_insight: Whoever owns the kill switch can price the tail. A capped, enforced exposure is a parametric insurance product, not an open-ended liability. Buyers are paying for certainty, and the tooling is only how you deliver it.
first_30_days: Ship an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible proxy with breakers. Sign 10 startups to a beta guarantee capped at about $2k per incident, backed by a roughly $20k reserve. Price at about 4% of spend and log every incident. Talk to two parametric or MGA capacity providers.

title: Pay the Grandmother: Relative-Care Subsidy Enrollment
one_liner: A multilingual concierge plus verified-attendance software that turns unpaid grandparents and relatives into subsidy-paid, health-and-safety-cleared caregivers, billed per enrollment to states and referral agencies.
customer: State child-care subsidy (CCDF) lead agencies, county subsidy offices and child care resource and referral (CCR&R) agencies. Secondary: workforce boards and Head Start grantees.
problem: Deserts are measured in licensed slots (3+ kids per slot), but most parents actually cobble together relative care that the maps never count. Many states can already pay license-exempt relatives through subsidy. Families don't enroll because of fingerprinting, training, provider agreements and slow payment. States are also wary of fraud (federal subsidy-fraud scrutiny in winter 2025-26, from memory, not verified). So the 'supply' looks empty while grandmothers work for free.
solution: A guided onboarding flow in the caregiver's language covers document collection, fingerprint appointment booking, CPR and safe-sleep micro-training, and e-signed provider agreements. Attendance is logged by phone tap-in with geo-stamp and parent co-sign, which gives the state verified attendance. Payment goes out by direct deposit or prepaid card within days. A state dashboard shows 'real supply unlocked' by county.
why_now: Childcare costs hit about $13,128 a year (up 29% since 2020) while licensed supply barely grows (centers +1.5%, homes +4.3% in 2024). The 2024 federal CCDF rule (7% copay cap, enrollment-based prospective payment) is being implemented by states in 2025-26 (from memory). Universal-care promises (NYC per the brief) create demand for supply that needs no buildings. Fraud scrutiny makes verified attendance a selling point, not a cost.
revenue_model: Per completed enrollment fee ($150-400) plus a per-active-caregiver monthly fee ($3-8), paid by the agency under a pilot contract. Pilots run $30-60k per CCR&R or county.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in childcare deserts is not buildings or workers. It is unpaid supply that already exists, blocked by paperwork and by states' fear of fraud. The winner sells verified attendance as much as enrollment.
first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive relative-care rules. Map every enrollment step and drop-off point. Offer one CCR&R a free 25-family concierge pilot run over WhatsApp and phone, with Twilio and a no-code form behind it. Recruit through Spanish-, Somali- and Hmong-speaking community groups. Get a letter of intent from one county for a paid per-enrollment fee.

title: Heirloom Fair-Division Engine for Sibling Estates
one_liner: Use a fair-division algorithm and a phone walkthrough to split a dead parent's belongings so nobody feels cheated.
customer: Executors (often the eldest child), estate attorneys, mediators and professional fiduciaries. Families pay $149-$399 per estate, or attorneys pay $99/month.
problem: Research on inheritance conflict (for example the University of Minnesota's 'Who Gets Grandma's Yellow Pie Plate?' work) finds sentimental personal property, not money, triggers most sibling fights. Executors improvise with turn-taking or a spreadsheet, distant siblings get shortchanged, and the house can't be sold until it is cleared.
solution: A phone walkthrough captures the house room by room, AI tags items, and each remote heir gets a private points budget to express wants. A fair-division algorithm (adjusted-winner or envy-free-up-to-one-item style) proposes an allocation with cash or point equalization. The app then coordinates shipping and pickup, and routes leftovers to donation with receipts or to sale. It ends with a signed distribution memo the attorney can file. Each item keeps a story card so its history survives.
why_now: Multimodal AI can inventory objects from video, and phone-based 3D capture is mainstream. Boomer households hold decades of belongings that Millennial and Gen X heirs scattered across the country often don't want. With the federal estate tax largely out of the picture for most families (reported $15M exemption), family conflict is the main remaining risk.
revenue_model: Per-estate fee ($149-$399), 10-15% margin on shipping and donation logistics, and attorney seats at $99/month.
non_obvious_insight: The fights are about objects, not dollars. Objects are one of the few asset classes with a known mechanism-design solution, and no estate product uses it.
first_30_days: Build a no-code prototype with a spreadsheet points auction. Offer it free to 20 executors found in estate-help forums and groups. Ask elder-law attorneys to use it as a mediation-lite deliverable and convert 5 of them to paid. Time-box the whole thing to about three weeks per estate.

title: Managed 24-Hour CRA Vulnerability Reporting Desk
one_liner: A hosted OWASP Dependency-Track plus an on-call analyst rota that tells small hardware makers within hours whether an exploited vulnerability hits their firmware, then drafts the ENISA 24h/72h filings.
customer: EU-selling makers of connected hardware with 5-250 staff and no product-security team (smart-home devices, e-bikes, EV chargers, industrial gateways, toys, wearables). Buyer is the CTO or regulatory/CE-marking manager. Secondary channel is CE-marking consultants who need a white-label reporting partner.
problem: The EU Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties went live on 11 Sept 2026. Manufacturers must send an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, then detail within 72 hours, through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. Fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers ship Yocto, OpenWrt, Zephyr, OpenSSL and FFmpeg stacks and often can't say what is inside a firmware image. Nobody on their team is awake on Sunday when a CISA KEV entry lands.
solution: Ingest CycloneDX/SPDX SBOMs into a managed Dependency-Track instance. For products with no SBOM, generate one from the firmware image with Syft, cdxgen or EMBA, using Ghidra for binary-only blobs. Watch CISA KEV, the EU vulnerability database and OSV continuously. A human analyst issues a VEX verdict (affected / not affected / under investigation) within hours. If affected, the desk pre-fills the SRP notification, drafts the customer advisory, and tracks the 24h, 72h and final-report clocks. The output is an auditable VEX history that a market-surveillance authority or notified body can read.
why_now: The 24-hour reporting clock started 11 Sept 2026 and the ENISA platform is open, so thousands of small makers are discovering they have weeks rather than the Dec 2027 date for full application. Dependency-Track and CycloneDX are the de facto open standards, but the paid options are enterprise appsec suites priced far above a 20-person hardware company's budget.
revenue_model: Retainer of EUR 300-1,500 per month per product family, tiered by number of firmware images and response-time SLA. One-off firmware SBOM generation at EUR 2-8k per image. Resale to CE consultants at a wholesale rate. Later add annual CRA technical-file support.
non_obvious_insight: Small manufacturers don't need another scanner, because the open-source plumbing already works. They need a human who can say 'not affected' with evidence inside 24 hours, because a false 'affected' filing is also costly. The scarce asset is analyst judgment plus a growing VEX history, which compounds across customers who share the same upstream components.
first_30_days: Stand up stock Dependency-Track and a KEV/EUVD watcher. Recruit 2-3 freelance embedded-security engineers for a shared on-call rota. Offer 20 free 'CRA exposure scans' (one firmware image in, one-page exposed-CVE report out) to IoT startups and to 100 CE-marking consultants found on LinkedIn and trade forums. Publish a weekly 'which exploited CVEs hit your Yocto/OpenWrt image' digest to build the list. Convert scans into 6-month retainers at a design-partner price.

title: Driver-Sourced Dock Queue Index for Funds
one_liner: Pay verified truckers to report what they see at plants, ports and distribution centers, and sell the resulting real-economy index to funds, credit analysts and site-selection teams.
customer: Small and mid-size quant and fundamental hedge funds, equity and credit research shops covering industrials and retail, private-credit lenders to retailers and manufacturers, and commercial real-estate investors. Annual subscriptions of $25k to $150k per sector index.
problem: Alt-data vendors see parking lots from satellites and card swipes from panels, but nobody sees the freight dock. Telematics vendors sell dwell time at a geofence but not what's moving, whether the yard is full, or whether appointments are being cancelled. Tariff shocks in 2025 to 2026 made import front-loading, steel inventory builds and retailer DC slowdowns critical to read weeks earlier. The alt-data market was about $2.8B in 2025 and most institutional funds use several sources, but trucking signals stay coarse.
solution: A watchlist of about 500 facilities mapped to public tickers (steel mills, Amazon and Walmart DCs, Home Depot and Costco DCs, auto plants, ports and rail ramps). Drivers whose ELD or phone geofence confirms they are at the site file a 30-second structured report: queue length, hours waited, outbound commodity, trailers stacked or pulled, yard fullness, appointments cancelled, 'no freight today'. Pay $3 to $8 per accepted report. Aggregate into weekly facility, sector and regional indices. Only publicly observable facts are collected, with no shipper confidential documents and no insider employees. A securities lawyer reviews the collection rules before launch.
why_now: Tariff-driven import and inventory swings make physical-economy signals more valuable than ever. Freight recession conditions mean lots of idle drivers willing to earn side income while waiting. Geofence verification, instant payouts and modern OCR/LLM structuring make a human-observation network cheap to run. Fund appetite for differentiated alt data is high because standard satellite and card data are commoditized.
revenue_model: Sector-index subscriptions of $30k to $150k a year, custom facility watchlists, a raw API tier, and per-project reports for private-credit lenders and site-selection teams. Drivers are paid per report, so unit economics are strongly positive.
non_obvious_insight: Truckers are the only people who physically stand in line at the real economy every day. A driver notices 'the mill's outbound lot is empty at 2pm Tuesday' or 'this DC is turning away appointments' weeks before it shows up in ISM or earnings. Telematics sells dwell minutes, but only a human sees the commodity mix, the closed dock doors and the mood in the queue, and drivers already trade this information on CB and in Facebook groups for free. This is a new data category, not an improvement to freight software.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 drivers across three freight regions (Gulf Coast, Midwest steel belt, Inland Empire) via Facebook groups and pay $5 per accepted report via instant payment. Cover 20 facilities weekly for 4 weeks. Backtest the index against public earnings and shipment data. Pitch 10 small funds through alt-data brokers and direct outreach with a free 30-day trial on 10 tickers. Charge $2k to $5k a month pilots after the trial.

title: Native-Language Translation Earpieces for Dementia Care
one_liner: Dementia-tuned real-time speech translation and a life-story phrasebook so aides can soothe residents in the language they reverted to.
customer: Memory-care communities and nursing homes with multilingual residents, and home-care agencies in NYC, Miami, LA, the Bay Area and Houston.
problem: People with dementia often revert to a first language, while 30% of care workers (60% in New York) are immigrants who speak other languages. The mismatch causes agitation, missed pain, more antipsychotic use and hospital transfers. Compliance-grade phone interpreters are too slow for a 3 am redirect.
solution: An earbud and tablet kit with speech-to-speech translation tuned for dementia (short, slow, warm, repetitive), a preloaded ADL and redirection phrasebook, resident life-story cards in their language (hometown, family, songs), and a video human-interpreter fallback within 30 seconds. Staff dashboards report agitation and PRN antipsychotic use.
why_now: Real-time on-device speech translation reached mainstream earbuds and phones in 2025-26, while visa and TPS shocks are replacing staff with workers who share fewer languages with residents.
revenue_model: $30-60 per resident per month, or $99 per aide per month, plus an implementation fee.
non_obvious_insight: Language access is treated as a compliance checkbox, not a clinical tool. Generic translation isn't tuned to dementia speech and emotion, and the measurable outcome (fewer PRN antipsychotics) is a metric operators already care about.
first_30_days: Identify five memory-care communities with Spanish-, Russian- or Chinese-speaking residents. Run $500 pilots with tablets and an interpreter fallback, and measure PRN antipsychotic use before and after.

title: Fake-Citation Triage for Defendants Facing Pro Se Filings
one_liner: A same-day report showing which citations in an opposing pro se filing are fake, misquoted or overruled, formatted as a court-ready exhibit for a motion to strike or for sanctions.
customer: Repeat defendants that get flooded with self-represented suits: landlord and property-management litigation groups, employment-defense boutiques, university and hospital counsel, insurer claims-litigation units, debt servicers, city attorney offices and municipal risk pools. Paid by the litigation budget owner.
problem: Charlotin's database holds about 2,095 AI-hallucination cases as of 28 Sep 2026, and 1,208 (58%) involve pro se litigants versus 829 involving lawyers. Pro se filers are immune to bar discipline, sanctions ($1,750 to $23,222) are slow and rare, and the defendant pays $300-600/hour of associate time to hand-check dozens of cites. Every hallucination-checker on the market is pitched to the lawyer who erred.
solution: Drag-and-drop a PDF. The tool extracts citations (open-source eyecite plus CourtListener), resolves each one, and flags nonexistent cases, quotes that do not appear in the opinion, wrong court or year, and negative treatment. Output is a two-page 'Citation Defect Declaration' plus a draft paragraph for a motion to strike or a Rule 11-type motion. Phase two hooks into the e-service email inbox so every incoming filing is screened automatically.
why_now: The volume of fabricated-citation filings is now measured in the thousands and judges have seen enough to act on them. Open case-law data (CourtListener) is now good enough that OpenAI built Astra for Law on it (17 Sep 2026), so the verification corpus is cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: $49-149 per filing report self-serve, or $1,500-5,000/month flat for repeat defendants with inbox integration. Upsell is drafting of the sanctions or strike motion at a fixed fee.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer everyone targets (the erring lawyer) has a small budget and an embarrassment problem. The money and standing sit with the counterparty, who pays hourly to verify someone else's junk and is the only actor who can turn a bad cite into leverage (strike, fee-shifting, vexatious-litigant designation).
first_30_days: Build on eyecite and the CourtListener API, then benchmark accuracy on 100 known cases from the Charlotin database as ground truth. Cold-email 30 landlord-tenant and employment-defense firms and 10 municipal risk pools, offering 10 free reports in exchange for permission to attach a report to a filing. Charge $99 per report after that and aim for 3-5 recurring accounts.

title: Managed Runtime for Custom Apps Built for Local Businesses
one_liner: A white-label hosting, backup and "someone to call" layer for AI-built custom apps that freelancers and owners now build for small businesses.
customer: Two buyers. (a) Solo builders, freelancers and small agencies who build custom tools for local businesses, including failed micro-SaaS founders. They pay wholesale per app and mark it up. (b) Small business owners who built a tool themselves and want it kept alive.
problem: Builders and buyers have both moved off subscription SaaS, and reliability is now nobody's job. r/SaaS: "Customer cancelled after 18 months. Reason: 'We built it ourselves.'", "No one is going to pay for your vibe-coded SaaS", "Mass-produced AI apps for 14 months. Made $2,847 total. My friend sells pool cleaning services and cleared $94K.", "I wasted $50k because I thought the code was the expensive part." r/Entrepreneur (88/100): "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses." When the dispatch board or intake form breaks at 7am, nobody is answerable.
solution: 1) A one-click deploy of an AI-built app to a hardened runtime with auth, nightly backups, uptime checks, data export and secrets rotation. 2) Dependency and security patching. 3) A "break-glass" human fix within one business day, sold as credits. 4) Builders resell the bundle with their own markup, so they earn recurring revenue from boring customers instead of chasing SaaS signups. 5) The small business gets an SLA and a runbook in plain language.
why_now: In February 2026 nearly $1T was wiped from software and services valuations as coding agents made build-versus-buy tilt toward build (TechCrunch, Mar 1, 2026). Small customers are now building their own replacements, and thousands of AI-SaaS founders who cannot sell subscriptions are turning to service-style custom work.
revenue_model: $39-79 per app per month wholesale to builders, who charge clients $100-200/mo. Break-glass fix credits ($150 per incident). A $199/mo direct plan for owners who built their own tool.
non_obvious_insight: When code is cheap, the scarce thing is accountability: someone who answers when the tool breaks. The supply and demand are visible in the same threads: small customers churn because they built it themselves (r/SaaS, https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/saas), and r/Entrepreneur scores "The SaaS model is quietly falling apart for small businesses" at 88/100 (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/Entrepreneur). The macro shift toward build over buy is documented at https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/01/saas-in-saas-out-heres-whats-driving-the-saaspocalypse/. Honest caveat: the demand for the caretaking layer is inferred from these signals, not seen in a direct "I'd pay for" post, so the first month is a paid-demand test.
first_30_days: Week 1: DM 30 builders who posted about pivoting to "boring" service customers, and offer to host and maintain their existing client apps for $49. Weeks 2-3: onboard 10 real apps onto a standard stack (managed database, backups, uptime monitor, alerts) using off-the-shelf tooling. Week 4: sell the wholesale plan to the first 3 builders and log every incident to price break-glass credits. Kill test: fewer than 5 paying apps after 30 days means the pain is not there.

title: Certified SDE for Sub-$1M Business Sales
one_liner: A CPA-signed, AI-prepared earnings certificate that lets brokers, buyers and SBA lenders trust a small business's seller's discretionary earnings.
customer: Business brokers, SBA lenders and first-time buyers in $100k-$1M main-street deals, and the sellers who pay to be believed.
problem: A full quality-of-earnings review costs $15-50k, which is impossible on a $300k deal, so cash-heavy books and owner add-backs create distrust. Deals die in diligence or stall in lender underwriting. Search funds target $5-50M businesses and nothing standardizes trust for the smallest tier.
solution: Upload three years of returns, bank and processor statements and POS data. The system reconstructs revenue, recasts SDE with add-back evidence, and flags unrecorded revenue or personal expenses. A CPA signs a certified SDE range in 48 hours. Partner lenders accept the standard report, and it links to the escrow and route-sale flow.
why_now: SBA 7(a) plus 504 financing up to $10M began July 2026, so buyer demand and lender appetite are rising. LLMs and bank data make the reconstruction cheap.
revenue_model: $495-995 per report paid by the seller or broker, lender licensing, and buyer diligence upsells.
non_obvious_insight: At this size the bottleneck is neither buyers nor capital but trust in the earnings number. A QoE costs 5% of price, and a cheap certificate unlocks the whole tier.
first_30_days: Sign three brokers who list $200k-800k deals and produce 15 reports manually with a CPA. Ask one SBA lender in writing what it needs in order to accept the certificate.

title: Public Toilets as a Stipend Program, Not Construction
one_liner: A turnkey program manager that lets cities and business districts turn cafes, gyms, garages and gas stations into paid, insured and mapped public restrooms for a small annual stipend instead of building $225,000 freestanding toilets.
customer: Business improvement districts and downtown associations first (fast, budgeted, small contracts), then transit agencies, parks and public-works departments, and tourism boards.
problem: Public restrooms are a top complaint in every city and almost no one builds them because the capital and upkeep are brutal. One Portland Loo costs about $225,000 installed, and New York's 2026 pilot budgets about $4M for 17 units. Washington DC authorized a program to pay businesses to open their restrooms in 2018, but it went unfunded. Meanwhile there is a toilet on nearly every retail block behind a 'customers only' sign, because owners fear liability, cleaning cost and misuse, and nobody manages the risk.
solution: Run a managed 'Open Door' network. Recruit and contract the host businesses, pay a monthly stipend, provide a group liability rider or indemnity through a specialty insurance program, supply cleaning kits and signage, and put a QR code and map listing on each door. QR scans verify actual use, so cities pay for measured access and get council-ready reports on use by neighborhood and hour. A hotline handles complaints and revokes hosts who stop complying.
why_now: New York's very public 2026 pilot, including the 10-minute limit robotoilets, shows both political demand and sticker shock. Downtown business districts are fighting for foot traffic, homelessness and tourism pressure keeps restrooms a front-page issue, and smartphone QR verification makes pay-for-access measurable for the first time. Germany's Nette Toilette program has run in about 210 cities for years at roughly $34-$112 a month per business, so the model is proven but has not been productized in the US.
revenue_model: Program-management contract with the city or district: a setup fee plus about $600-$1,200 per site per year, with host stipends passed through at cost. A typical pilot of 15-20 sites is roughly $25-$60k a year. Add sponsorship by a host or utility brand and analytics subscriptions for tourism and transit boards.
non_obvious_insight: The expense of a public toilet is capital and ownership, not access. The scarce resource is liability-managed permission to use toilets that already exist. Whoever builds the group insurance, verification data and host-compliance system owns the market, and every city compares a $2,000-a-year stipend to a $225,000 kiosk.
first_30_days: Target two business improvement districts, which can approve $20-$50k pilots without a city-wide procurement cycle. Sign letters of intent from 15-20 hosts on the strongest blocks. Get a broker to quote a group liability rider. Print door stickers, build a one-page map with scan counts, and launch a 90-day pilot. Use week-4 scan data to ask the district to sign a 12-month contract and to open talks with the city.

title: Age-Signal Rules Engine for App Developers
one_liner: A 'feature-flag service for minors' law': an SDK that takes the OS or app-store age bracket plus jurisdiction and returns the legally required feature set, with citations and an audit trail.
customer: Mid-size consumer apps, games and edtech (10-500 staff) with under-18 users, their general counsel, and app agencies. Series A-C startups first.
problem: Texas app-store age verification (June 2026), Ohio consent (June 2026), Florida under-14 ban, California's OS age-attestation law, the UK regime, and bans in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia each define brackets and required behavior differently. Engineers hard-code rules and rules change monthly. Fines are large.
solution: A versioned policy graph maintained by lawyers plus LLM change tracking. The SDK returns flags for chat, DMs, push timing, ads, purchases and recommendation feeds per bracket and jurisdiction. It integrates with OS age-range signals and third-party verifiers and logs which rule applied when, for regulators.
why_now: For the first time OS and app stores hand developers an age signal (California signed Oct 2025; Apple and Google age-range APIs, from memory), but nobody says what to do with it. The 'policy ratchet' means fragmentation will grow.
revenue_model: $500-5k a month by MAU tier, plus one-time compliance-matrix audits at $3-6k.
non_obvious_insight: Age-verification vendors sell the signal, and nobody sells the decision: the legal mapping from signal to product behavior. That mapping is the durable moat because laws keep diverging.
first_30_days: Publish a public 8-jurisdiction by 5-feature matrix. Run a newsletter around it. Sell 5 compliance-matrix audits at $4k to game and app teams. Wrap the logic into an SDK by month 3.

title: Global Rain Radar From Starlink Dishes
one_liner: Turn opted-in Starlink terminals into the densest rain-gauge network ever built and sell ground-truth rainfall to insurers.
customer: Parametric crop and flood insurers and MGAs, reinsurers, agricultural cooperatives, utilities and municipal flood teams.
problem: Rain gauges are sparse and radar coverage is poor in rural and developing regions. Parametric insurance suffers from basis risk, and disputes arise when the index does not match what happened at the field.
solution: An open-source agent reads a terminal's local signal telemetry, correlates rain-induced attenuation with rain rate, and produces minute-level hyperlocal rainfall. Owners opt in and receive a monthly credit. Sell the result as an API and as audited trigger data for parametric products.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, including many rural users. The idea of using satellite-link attenuation as a rain sensor is established in research. Parametric insurance is growing, and public radar and gauge budgets are under pressure.
revenue_model: API subscriptions $20-200k per year per insurer or cooperative. Per-trigger data fees. Owner credits of $2-5 per month as the cost of goods.
non_obvious_insight: Rain fade is a nuisance to network engineers but a measurement to meteorologists. The sensors are already installed and paid for by their owners.
first_30_days: Adapt open-source telemetry tools and recruit 300 terminal owners with a small credit. Co-locate with 30 tipping-bucket gauges and publish a validation note. Pitch two parametric MGAs and one agricultural cooperative, and plan a fallback if SpaceX restricts local access.

title: Digital Legacy Setup Sold Through Wealth Advisors
one_liner: A white-labeled 'digital safety and legacy' visit for advisors' 80+ clients, paid for by the advisor as a retention and heir-acquisition tool.
customer: Independent RIAs and trust departments with $100M-$2B in assets and many clients over 78, plus elder-law attorneys as a secondary channel.
problem: Industry surveys often find that a majority of heirs fire their parents' advisor after an inheritance. Regulators also expect vigilance on senior clients, with trusted-contact requirements (FINRA 4512) and hold authority (Rule 2165). Meanwhile the 80-year-old's digital life (email, photos, passwords, crypto, cloud accounts, carrier, bank portals) is unmanaged. When they die or lose capacity the family can't get in, and scammers can.
solution: A 90-minute in-home or video visit by a trained 'digital steward': account inventory, password manager and passkey setup, Apple Legacy Contact and Google Inactive Account Manager set up, carrier port-out locks and credit freezes, bank alerts with 2FA routed to a trusted contact, and a family emergency binder handed to the heir or trustee. The heir joins the final visit, introduced by the advisor as the person who organized it. Add an annual re-check.
why_now: The multi-trillion-dollar generational wealth transfer is underway. More wealth sits in crypto and online accounts. Deepfake voice-clone scams target seniors. Apple and Google have shipped legacy-contact features but adoption is low, and FINRA's 2026 oversight report keeps trusted-contact practices in focus.
revenue_model: $450-900 per client visit paid by the advisor, who may pass it through, plus a $150/yr maintenance subscription. Referral fees from elder-law attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: The payer isn't the 80-year-old. It's the advisor, whose most valuable asset, the client relationship, is about to leave with the heirs. A digital steward visit is a useful favor that puts the advisor in the room with the next generation, and it doubles as compliance-friendly protection.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-10 RIAs through one advisor community (XYPN or local FPA chapters) and offer 3 free client visits each in exchange for feedback and a signed pilot. Hire retired IT pros or college students and train them on a checklist. Track how many heirs attend and whether advisors get follow-up meetings.

title: One Recert: Housing Paperwork Keeps Medicaid Coverage
one_liner: Reuse the income and employment paperwork affordable-housing operators already collect every year to stop residents' Medicaid from lapsing under the new work requirements, paid per retained member by Medicaid health plans.
customer: Medicaid managed-care organizations in expansion states (pay per retained member-month or per completed redetermination), plus LIHTC/HUD affordable-housing owners (pay per unit for lower delinquency and turnover). Hospitals in expansion states are a third payer.
problem: Work requirements hit all 41 expansion states on Jan 1, 2027 (Nebraska has been live since May 1, 2026), with 5.5-6.3M projected coverage losses and a 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hit to hospitals. Losses are mostly paperwork failures rather than true ineligibility (Arkansas's 2018 experiment saw about 18,000 people drop off largely through reporting failures). Each lost member is lost capitation for the plan, unpaid bills for the hospital and, later, a late-rent risk for the landlord.
solution: With resident consent, ingest the annual and interim income/employment verifications that housing operators already gather. Map them to state rules (80 hours a month, or roughly $580 in monthly income, plus exemptions such as caregivers), build the compliance packet, submit it to the state portal or plan, and send monthly nudges when hours dip. A remote call team plus the property's resident-services coordinator handles the human steps.
why_now: The Jan 1, 2027 nationwide deadline is three months away and plans are setting 2027 retention budgets now. Nebraska is a live proving ground today. ACA subsidy expiry already added about 4.8M uninsured, so plans and hospitals are hunting for any lever that keeps members covered.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month retention fee or $75-150 per completed redetermination from plans; $2-4/unit/month SaaS from housing owners; hospital-funded pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Affordable-housing recertification is the most audit-grade employment and income record low-income adults have, and nobody reuses it. The housing operator is also the only party that sees the resident monthly and has its own reason to care, since Medicaid loss leads to medical debt and then late rent.
first_30_days: Start in Nebraska. Sign one affordable operator with 1,000-3,000 units and one Medicaid plan. Hand-build the packet workflow with forms and spreadsheets for 100 consenting residents, measure retention against a comparison group, and price the service per retained member. Clone state by state ahead of Jan 1.

title: Pay-on-Green: Escrow Released by Executable Tests
one_liner: Escrow for agent-to-agent work where the negotiated object is a hashed acceptance test, and money moves only when the test passes.
customer: Growth, data and ops teams at 20-500 person companies that subcontract bulk deliverables (data enrichment, scraping, code migrations, translation with QA) to other vendors' agents, plus the small agent vendors who want guaranteed payment.
problem: Card chargebacks do not fit machine-speed commerce and stablecoin payments are irreversible. The dispute in agent work is almost always 'was it good enough?', and no human can review thousands of small deliverables. The 2026 payment protocols (AP2, ACP, x402, MPP) settle payment but say little about quality or delayed fulfilment.
solution: A 'test-as-contract' escrow. Before work starts, buyer and seller agents agree on an executable acceptance suite: schema and checksum checks, unit tests, planted canary items with known answers, and a rubric graded by a panel of three different-model judges with pre-committed prompts. Funds lock in escrow. On delivery the suite runs in a sandbox and releases funds item by item (partial settlement). Disputes narrow to 'was the test fair?' and go to a small-claims panel with human appeal. Third parties publish reusable verifier suites and earn a royalty per run.
why_now: Agents in 2026 routinely delegate subtasks to other vendors' agents. LLM-as-judge and cheap sandboxes are mature. Four competing payment protocols now exist, and academic proposals for refundable, delayed-fulfilment settlement (for example the Agentic Settlement Protocol paper of September 2026) show the dispute layer is an acknowledged gap.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% escrow fee on GMV, plus $0.01-0.05 per verifier run, plus a royalty share to verifier authors. Enterprise plan with SLAs and private test libraries.
non_obvious_insight: Move the dispute before the money moves. Agents will not argue price, they will argue the test, so the durable asset is a growing library of standard acceptance suites, which works like an ISO standard for agent deliverables. Planted canaries (honeypot items, as crowdsourcing platforms use) catch lazy or fraudulent sellers cheaply.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical where canaries are easy: bulk lead-list verification and web-data extraction. Recruit 5 small agent vendors and 3 buyers from indie-hacker and MCP developer communities. Run escrow manually on Stripe Connect with delayed payouts. Publish 20 open-source acceptance-test templates as lead magnets. Charge 3% and aim for $10k of escrowed GMV.

title: Group Apprenticeship Employer for Data-Center Electricians
one_liner: An Australian-style group training organization that employs apprentices and rents them to small electrical and plumbing contractors, absorbing the paperwork, wage risk and poaching risk.
customer: Small and mid-size electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors (5-50 staff) in data-center and construction-boom metros; apprentices, including underemployed college grads.
problem: Electricians have about 72.7k openings a year, boosted by data-center demand, but the 4-5 year path is bottlenecked by employer sponsors and pre-apprenticeship screening. Small contractors cannot carry multi-year risk, admin and classroom scheduling, and apprentices are poached after year one or two. Meanwhile 42% of recent grads are underemployed and have no route in.
solution: The group sponsor is the registered-apprenticeship sponsor and employer of record. It screens and recruits, pays wages and workers' comp, rotates apprentices across host contractors, schedules related instruction with a community college or JATC (up to 49% of instruction can be outsourced to employers or unions under the new apprenticeship rules), and bills hosts hourly. Market a career-changer track to laid-off grads.
why_now: AI data-center construction is pulling electricians while AI is closing entry-level white-collar doors, creating both demand and a motivated recruit pool. Workforce Pell gives apprenticeship-linked programs a fast lane, making college partners eager.
revenue_model: A 20-30% markup over apprentice wage cost billed to host contractors (about 15-20% gross margin, staffing-style), plus state apprenticeship incentives and college partnership fees.
non_obvious_insight: Contractors do not lack applicants; they lack appetite for multi-year risk and administration. Splitting the employer role from the host job site removes the constraint, as group training organizations did in Australia.
first_30_days: Choose one data-center metro. Sign 5 small contractors to LOIs for 10 apprentice seats. Partner with an existing IEC or ABC chapter for registration and compliance. Recruit 30 candidates from local underemployed grads and start an 8-week evening pre-apprenticeship course.

title: Own-Your-Office Buyer Groups for Practices
one_liner: Assemble dentists, clinics, law and accounting firms into buyer clubs that buy discounted vacant office buildings and split them into owner-occupied condos financed with SBA loans.
customer: Small professional practices renting 3,000-15,000 sf each (5-20 per building), plus special servicers and receivers who need a bulk exit for distressed office.
problem: National office vacancy is 17.8%, office CMBS delinquency 13.2%, $39B of office debt matures within 12 months and $289B by 2028 on about 14,000 properties. Sellers are forced, but institutional buyers price office as an income asset and few small buyers can act. Small practices keep paying roughly $33 asking rent with escalators and never see the building trade at a fraction of replacement cost.
solution: Pre-qualify 8-15 owner-users (financials and SBA 504/7(a) eligibility), find 40-150k sf Class B buildings from servicers at low per-sf bases, create a condo declaration and a single purchasing entity, close in bulk, then finance and deed units individually to practices (each occupying its own space). Keep the association-management and repositioning contract.
why_now: Servicers are actively seeking exits and most B/C buildings do not pencil for residential conversion, so owner-occupancy is the highest and best use. SBA programs finance owner-occupants at very high LTV, and high rates make a lease a large fixed cost relative to ownership.
revenue_model: 2-4% sponsor fee per unit sold, condo-ization margin or promote on unsold units, and recurring building/association management ($0.60-1.00 per sf per year) plus resale commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Investors value office on cash-flow multiples, while owner-users value it at the rent they would otherwise pay. At distressed bases the owner-user's willingness to pay can exceed the investor's bid, and no one is aggregating this fragmented demand against a forced-seller supply pool.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with cheap Class B office. Launch a landing page and outreach through dental, medical and CPA associations and SBA/CDC lenders. Collect 10 non-binding letters of intent from practices. Approach 2-3 servicer asset managers about bulk-sale listings. Charge a refundable $2,500 deposit for founding-member slots.

title: Programmable Lockbox for GPU and Robot Collateral
one_liner: Tri-party custody software and hardware that lets lenders verify, and if needed take over, financed GPU clusters and robot fleets sitting in someone else's building.
customer: Specialty and private-credit lenders and equipment lessors financing GPU clouds and robots-as-a-service. Borrowers such as neoclouds and robot operators pay to lower their borrowing spread, and colo operators act as a channel.
problem: More than $20B of loans are now secured by GPUs, and H100-class rental rates fell from about $7-10 per hour in early 2024 to $2-4 by late 2025, so lenders must know whether machines exist, are powered and utilised, and are not double-pledged. Monitoring today is a spreadsheet plus quarterly audits. The bigger trapdoors are the colo landlord's lien for unpaid power or rent and who physically or remotely controls the hardware on default.
solution: (1) A continuous collateral-health feed: hardware serials and attestation (TPM or GPU attestation where available), BMC and out-of-band data, power-meter readings, latency-based geolocation, and periodic photo audits by colo remote hands. (2) Escrowed step-in credentials for BMC and fleet consoles, plus a tri-party lockbox agreement with the colo covering access and lien waivers, with API-triggered 'freeze' and 'transfer to lender' modes. (3) Standard borrowing-base reports.
why_now: GPU-collateralised private credit scaled from almost nothing to over $20B in about two years, with loans maturing 2026-2028 among a small, correlated lender group. Banks avoid the fast-depreciating collateral, leaving private credit to fill the gap. Utilisation and location risk is now board-level for lenders. Robot-as-a-service leasing needs the same control layer.
revenue_model: $15-40 per GPU or robot per month paid by the borrower, or 10-25 bps on outstanding facility size, plus a $25k onboarding fee per facility and colo referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Lender losses come from control failures such as liens, access and double-pledging, not from chips vanishing. Contracts plus access-control APIs solve most of it. The borrower is the real buyer, because a 50-100 bps lower spread beats the fee, so sell it to the neocloud CFO as a rate reduction.
first_30_days: Speak with 15 specialty lenders and equipment-finance boutiques and 10 GPU-cloud CFOs. Sell a manual 'collateral control audit' at $15-30k for two facilities. Draft the tri-party lockbox template with a finance lawyer, then productise the attestation feed.

title: Cremation Memorial Rooms in Vacant Office Space
one_liner: Pay-per-event celebration-of-life rooms in empty ground-floor and office space for families choosing cremation, with an optional urn-niche wall run through a licensed cemetery partner as the long-term annuity.
customer: Families arranging cremation memorials, and direct-cremation providers and independent funeral homes without a venue. Landlords, lenders and special servicers with vacant space earn a revenue share. A licensed cemetery or church partner operates the niches.
problem: Cremation is about 63% of dispositions and heading to 82% by 2045, so the traditional chapel is redundant, but families still need somewhere to gather and somewhere to keep the ashes. 58% of consumers have attended a service at an unconventional venue, and families pay $2-5K for hotel ballrooms and restaurants. Office vacancy is 17.8% nationally, office CMBS delinquency is 13.2% with $39B maturing within 12 months, and urban cemeteries are out of land.
solution: Lease or license vacant space on short terms and fit it out as a 40-80 seat memorial room with AV for tribute video, catering and celebrant partners. Sell event packages wholesale to direct-cremation and funeral-home partners and directly to families ($1,500-3,500). In phase 2, add a niche wall sold as perpetual-care niches through a licensed cemetery operator, since a niche needs a fraction of the land of a burial plot. Zoning and state cemetery law vary, so licensing runs through the partner.
why_now: Cremation crossed 60% and consumer interest in alternatives is rising. Special servicers of distressed office loans will take short-term income from otherwise dead space. Direct-cremation providers are crowded and need a differentiator beyond price. SCI is growing on pricing while volumes fall, which leaves the low-cost end unserved.
revenue_model: Event fees, wholesale packages for funeral homes and direct-cremation providers, a 10-20% commission or operating share on niche sales, and landlord revenue-share deals. Later, employer celebration-of-life benefits.
non_obvious_insight: Cremation removed the need for the funeral home's most expensive asset, the chapel and its land, but not the human need to gather and to keep remains, which now needs roughly one fiftieth of the space. That makes converted office and retail space, not a cemetery, the right home.
first_30_days: Get a 90-day pop-up license for a vacant ground floor in a mid-size downtown. Sign two celebrants and a caterer. Offer wholesale rates to five direct-cremation providers and run three events at cost. Meet a licensed cemetery operator to scope the niche-wall pilot and the state licensing path.

title: Robotaxi Revenue-at-Risk Ratings for Airports and Cities
one_liner: A quarterly exposure index and analyst service that estimates how much airport parking, meter and citation revenue, and the bonds backed by it, will erode as robotaxis scale city by city.
customer: Municipal bond investors and credit research desks, rating and bond insurance analysts, airport and city CFOs and parking operators, and regional lenders holding parking-heavy real estate collateral.
problem: Parking and ground transportation account for roughly 43-45% of airports' non-aeronautical revenue in North America. Waymo now serves Phoenix, San Jose, SFO (curbside) and San Antonio, where a round-trip robotaxi fare of $15-25 undercuts the $30-150 an airport earns on a multi-day parking stay. Cities depend on meters and citations, and garage cash flows collateralize loans. Nobody underwrites this transition; disclosures are scattered across PDFs.
solution: Structure the data from airport financial reports, bond official statements and city ACFRs, then combine it with AV service-area maps, expansion announcements, ride-hail share and ground-transport fee schedules. Publish per-airport and per-city 'percentage of revenue at risk' under three adoption scenarios, plus fee-design advice (AV-specific trip fees, dynamic parking). Ship a free public index to build authority, then sell subscriptions, alerts and consulting.
why_now: Waymo reports 500k paid weekly rides, launched Denver, San Diego and Tampa on September 1 (14 commercial cities), and targets 1M weekly rides by year-end. LAX is already raising per-trip TNC fees to $6. Airports and cities are scrambling for a playbook and investors have no model.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-40k per year for buy-side and rating shops, $25-100k consulting engagements with airports and cities, and custom risk screens for lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The first place AVs bite public finance is not jobs, it is the parking-fee cash flows pledged to bonds that everyone treats as stable. The data is public but unstructured, so a two-person team with careful extraction can build a moat before larger research houses look.
first_30_days: Extract parking and ground-transport revenue lines for the top 30 US airports and 20 cities from public reports. Build a simple three-scenario model and publish a free index and a short note. Send it to 50 muni credit analysts and airport finance officers and sell the first five paid subscriptions.

title: Withholding-Credit Reconciliation for Indonesian Sellers
one_liner: Reconcile marketplace-withheld tax against annual returns for the many small sellers across Shopee, TikTok Shop and Tokopedia.
customer: Indonesian SME marketplace sellers and the bookkeepers who serve them.
problem: Indonesia starts marketplace tax collection on Oct 1 and has cut de minimis to $3. Sellers on several platforms will see withheld amounts on payouts, and matching those to annual filings creates over- and under-payment risk.
solution: Ingest payout statements and withholding proofs by API or WhatsApp forward, reconcile per platform, flag threshold crossings and generate return workpapers. The wedge is a white-label tool for accountants who serve seller communities.
why_now: The Oct 1 start date forces this pain within a quarter. Details of the rules should be verified before building.
revenue_model: Rp99-299k per month per seller, or an accountant white-label licence.
non_obvious_insight: Platform collection makes compliance visible, and a seller's first pain is reconciling rather than filing. The accountant channel is fragmented and unserved.
first_30_days: Support one platform's statement format and recruit 50 sellers through seller WhatsApp groups.
